clinicalPearls: Non-obstructive azoospermia is the absence of ejaculated sperm due to failed or severely impaired sperm production rather than a blockage
The typical picture is of small, soft testes with a raised follicle-stimulating hormone, reflecting loss of the negative feedback normally provided by an intact germinal epithelium
This contrasts with obstructive azoospermia, where testicular volume and follicle-stimulating hormone are normal, and the distinction guides the entire management pathway
Recognised causes include Klinefelter syndrome, Y-chromosome microdeletions, prior cryptorchidism, gonadotoxic chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and idiopathic testicular failure
Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis are essential, both to establish a cause and because certain deletions predict whether surgical sperm retrieval is likely to succeed
Despite globally impaired production, focal areas of spermatogenesis may persist, so microdissection testicular sperm extraction can recover sperm in a meaningful proportion of men
Any retrieved sperm are used with intracytoplasmic sperm injection, and genetic counselling is important given the heritable causes
A trial of hormonal optimisation may be considered in selected men with a secondary (hypogonadotropic) component before retrieval
reference.pathophysiology: Non-obstructive azoospermia results from a primary failure of the seminiferous epithelium to produce sperm in sufficient numbers to appear in the ejaculate, with a patent excurrent duct system. The spectrum of histology ranges from maturation arrest to hypospermatogenesis and complete germ-cell aplasia (Sertoli-cell-only pattern). Because functioning germ cells are reduced or absent, inhibin feedback falls and pituitary follicle-stimulating hormone rises, while the testes lose volume and become soft. Underlying mechanisms include chromosomal disorders such as Klinefelter syndrome, deletions of the azoospermia factor regions of the Y chromosome, the aftermath of undescended testes, and damage from cytotoxic treatment, though many cases remain idiopathic. Even in severely affected testes, spermatogenesis can be patchy, which underpins the rationale for meticulous surgical exploration.
additionalDifferentials: Klinefelter syndrome and other chromosomal disorders
History of cryptorchidism or testicular torsion
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism producing a secretory picture with low gonadotropins
additionalInvestigations: Repeat centrifuged semen analysis to confirm the absence of sperm
Serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, and testosterone, with a raised follicle-stimulating hormone supporting spermatogenic failure
Karyotype to detect Klinefelter syndrome and other chromosomal abnormalities
Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis to establish cause and guide retrieval prospects
Scrotal ultrasound to assess testicular volume and exclude associated pathology
Prolactin and, where a central cause is suspected, pituitary assessment
Diagnostic and therapeutic testicular sperm extraction, ideally by microdissection technique
redFlags: A testicular mass detected on examination or ultrasound
Features of Klinefelter syndrome prompting broader endocrine and metabolic surveillance
A complete azoospermia-factor deletion predicting little chance of retrievable sperm
Signs of a pituitary lesion where gonadotropins are inappropriately low
reference.prognosis: The reproductive outlook is more guarded than in obstructive disease, but microdissection testicular sperm extraction retrieves usable sperm in a substantial minority to allow fatherhood through intracytoplasmic sperm injection; the likelihood is influenced by the underlying cause and specific genetic findings.
pitfalls: Failing to differentiate non-obstructive from obstructive azoospermia by integrating testicular size with follicle-stimulating hormone
Omitting karyotype and Y-microdeletion testing before attempting retrieval
Proceeding to sperm extraction without genetic counselling about heritable causes
Assuming no sperm can be found and denying a man a properly performed microdissection retrieval
Overlooking a treatable secondary hypogonadotropic component
references: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen
European Association of Urology guidelines on sexual and reproductive health
management: Identify and correct contributory factors, withdrawing gonadotoxic agents where possible and treating any endocrine abnormality, with gonadotrophin therapy where a hypogonadotropic cause is found
The principal route to biological fatherhood is microdissection testicular sperm extraction to recover focal sperm, used with intracytoplasmic sperm injection
Perform genetic testing and counselling before retrieval, with karyotype for Klinefelter syndrome and Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis, which predict retrieval success and heritable risk

Consider hormonal optimisation with agents such as aromatase inhibitors, selective oestrogen-receptor modulators or human chorionic gonadotrophin in selected men to improve the intratesticular milieu before retrieval
Cryopreserve any sperm recovered at surgery to maximise assisted-reproduction attempts
Counsel the couple on alternatives should retrieval fail, including donor insemination and adoption, with psychological support throughout
Manage within an andrology and reproductive medicine multidisciplinary team
